transcription.tex: The quadratic formula\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\par has no real value when the discriminant is negative. Introducing \(i\), with \(i^2=-1\), lets us express these roots.
Complex numbers arose in sixteenth-century work on polynomial equations, including Cardano’s work.

\(i=\sqrt{-1}\).\par An imaginary number has form \(bi\), \(b\in\mathbb R\), such as \(i,3i,-2i,\pi i\).\par A complex number has form \(a+bi\), \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), such as \(1+i,3-2i\). Its real part is \(a\) and its imaginary part is \(b\).

\textbf{Notation}\par Coefficients usually precede constants and variables, as in \(2\pi x\) or \(3\pi ix\). Both \(a+bi\) and \(a+ib\) are valid: multiplication commutes.\par The conventional form of Euler’s formula is \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), with special case \(e^{i\pi}+1=0\). Writing \(e^{\theta i}\) is mathematically equivalent.

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Fractals}\par The Mandelbrot set is a famous fractal. We will investigate its recurrence later in this chapter.

\textbf{2. Analytic number theory}\par Number theory studies integers. Analytic methods use real and complex variables; for example, the Riemann zeta function accepts complex inputs and is linked to the distribution of primes.
\textbf{3. Physics and engineering}\par Applications include signal analysis, quantum mechanics, fluid dynamics, relativity and control theory.

transcription.tex: \textbf{How does the Mandelbrot set work?}\par Recurrences: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+2,x_1=0\) gives \(0,2,4,\ldots\), diverging.\par \(x_{n+1}=5+x_n/2,x_1=0\) gives \(0,5,7.5,8.75,\ldots\), converging to 10.\par For the Mandelbrot set, use\[z_{n+1}=z_n^2+c,\quad z_1=0.\]

Plot \(a+bi\) at \((a,b)\) on an Argand diagram (chapter 2). The Mandelbrot set consists of the values of \(c\) whose sequence stays bounded. Bounded sequences need not converge or repeat.\par Thus \(i\), plotted at \((0,1)\), belongs to the set; 1, at \((1,0)\), does not.
Considering every \(c\) produces the fractal boundary. Colours outside the set can show escape speed; black indicates bounded behaviour in this illustration.

slides.title: Why Non-real Roots Come in Conjugate Pairs

transcription.tex: Prove non-real roots of a quadratic with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs.\par \textbf{Proof 1: quadratic formula}

For real \(a,b,c\), \(a\ne0\), suppose \(b^2-4ac<0\).\[z=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\[=-\frac b{2a}\pm\frac{\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\[=-\frac b{2a}\pm\frac{\sqrt{4ac-b^2}}{2a}i.\]\par The real parts are equal and imaginary parts opposite: the roots are conjugates.

\(\alpha+\beta\) and \(\alpha\beta\) must be real. Put \(\alpha=a_1+b_1i,\beta=a_2+b_2i\).\par \(\alpha+\beta=(a_1+a_2)+(b_1+b_2)i\). From the sum, \(b_1+b_2=0\), so \(b_2=-b_1\).\[\alpha\beta=(a_1a_2-b_1b_2)+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1)i.\]\par Its imaginary part vanishes:\[-a_1b_1+a_2b_1=b_1(a_2-a_1)=0.\]\par Either \(b_1=b_2=0\) (both roots real), or \(a_2=a_1\) and \(b_2=-b_1\), proving conjugacy for non-real roots.
